attack_type: Unknown Anomaly - Potential Zero-Day or Novel Threat
rag_semantic_descriptions: The network traffic deviates significantly from the established normal baseline but does not match any known attack signature in the database, suggesting a potential zero-day exploit or novel technique.
The machine learning model has flagged this traffic with a high anomaly score or reconstruction error, indicating it is statistically improbable based on the normal training data.
A sudden, massive spike in traffic to a service that normally sees low utilization has broken historical time-series baselines without matching any known attack profile.

Services are communicating over unexpected or non-standard port combinations — for example, SSH-like traffic over port 443 or database queries leaving the external firewall — suggesting possible tunneling.
Packets are arriving with illegal, malformed, or highly unusual TCP flag combinations like simultaneous SYN/FIN/RST flags that are designed to confuse network inspection appliances.
This anomaly could be caused by new software deployments, infrastructure migrations, or unexpectedly popular new services that naturally break old baseline models until retraining occurs.
A hardware failure, misconfigured router, or network loop may be generating chaotic traffic patterns that the anomaly detection system is correctly identifying as abnormal.
The specific SHAP feature contributors vary wildly depending on the nature of the novelty, making this a catch-all classification requiring immediate manual investigation.
Protocol behavior analysis shows traffic that violates standard RFC specifications, suggesting either a deliberately crafted evasion technique or severely malfunctioning network equipment.
This classification serves as an early warning system — while it may be a false positive from infrastructure changes, it could also be the first indicator of a previously unseen attack method.
